source.title: Adam Improves Muon: Adaptive Moment Estimation with Orthogonalized Momentum
source.authors: Min-Xin Zhang; Yuxuan Liu; Hayden Schaeffer

record.tranche_reason: Reports GPT-2 language-model pretraining results comparing optimizer choices using training and validation losses, extending optimizer comparisons to this setting.
record.gate_note: The study does not test the listed versions: it does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD, vary batch size, or measure training-to-test error gaps. It reports optimizer-specific GPT-2 training and validation losses; these bear on generalization performance but fit none of V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study discusses Adam's adverse generalization as motivation, but its own results test none of V1–V8. It compares AdamW, Muon, NAMO and NAMO-D without an SGD or momentum-SGD comparator. Validation loss measures held-out performance; the missing V4 comparison, rather than the use of loss instead of accuracy, prevents a verdict. Its batch-size theory concerns optimization convergence, not held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors establish optimal deterministic convergence rates under their assumptions and noise-dependent stochastic bounds attaining the optimal rate with sufficiently large batches. They report lower GPT-2 training and validation losses for NAMO and NAMO-D than AdamW and Muon, with further gains from NAMO-D's clamping parameter.
record.recipe_differences: GPT-2 pretraining on OpenWebText compares AdamW and Muon with newly proposed norm-adaptive orthogonalized optimizers; no original claim intervention is reproduced.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by optimizer and GPT-2 model size; NAMO-D results also depend on the clamping parameter, which was fixed at 0.1 for GPT-2 (124M) and selected by a sweep for GPT-2 (355M).

fits_no_version.finding: At the reported endpoints, NAMO and NAMO-D achieve lower training and validation losses than AdamW and Muon for both GPT-2 sizes; NAMO-D also improves on NAMO.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With the selected hyperparameters on OpenWebText, NAMO and NAMO-D improve endpoint GPT-2 training and validation losses over AdamW and Muon.

record.problems: The empirical comparison is limited to two GPT-2 sizes and one dataset; training lengths differ by size (50K versus 10K steps). No uncertainty estimates are reported. Validation loss is reported, not test error or the training-to-test gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy under matched recipes.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed to fit the training data.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive methods versus SGD or momentum SGD, including tuning, weight-decay and switching qualifications.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized versus randomly selected examples.

record.verdict_notes: All numerical rows match Table 2, but they are out-of-scope method-performance benchmarks rather than evidence for V1–V8. Learning rates were selected using validation loss; GPT-2 (355M) NAMO-D additionally received a clamping-parameter sweep. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The citation to Wilson et al. supplies background, not an independent test of V4.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test accuracy.
Width sweep past interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD; broader tuning, switching, and weight-decay conditions.
Large versus small batch under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
